newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN RULES - Best on Ground - Andrew Bartram's Aussie Rules column.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN RULES - Best on Ground - Andrew Bartram's Aussie Rules column.

text.p: DOGS ON THE MARCH TO SEPTEMBER

For much of this AFL season the hitherto unfashionable Western Bulldogs have been accorded little credibility. But after 13 rounds and a tenacious 17-point win over St Kilda at Waverley Park on Saturday, the Bulldogs have announced themselves as a real premiership chance.
Now a game clear on top, Terry Wallace's team has shown that what counts is not the dog in the fight but the fight in the dog. Or, in Mike Tyson's case, the bite in the dog.
On a weekend when professional boxing lost all respect, some Richmond fans fared little better when they booed coach Robert Walls after the Tigers' 93-point thrashing by Essendon.
In a return to the grim dark days of the late 80s and early 90s, the Tigers slumped to second last on the ladder with an unspirited performance against the improving Bombers.

In accepting the blame for the loss, Walls' position as coach looks almost untenable and unless the Tigers can improve rapidly, he will be looking for a new job, possibly before the end of the season.
After the game a shattered Walls said his team played poorly and without much aggression at the football.
"It hurts because you put a lot into it (and) we gave virtually nothing today, so it's devastating," he said.
The Bombers, rocked by the defection to Melbourne of trusted football manager Danny Corcoran days earlier, kept their slim finals chances alive with their first win since May 3.
Corcoran would not have taken long to realise the enormity of his new task had he ventured to Waverley Park on Sunday where Hawthorn thrashed the Demons by 63 points.

Hawk full back Chris Langord returned to the fray as if he had never left with 20 possessions while the successful return of David Neitz and Sahun Smith from long-term injuries was a fillip for the depleted Demons.
Atrocious ground conditions at the SCG turned Sunday's grand final replay between Sydney and North Melbourne into a virtual mud wrestle.
The Swans trailed by five points at the last change but rallied to win by 10 points in a fitting result for skipper Paul Kelly's 150th game.
North captain Wayne Carey, returning from a 12 week injury lay off for his 150th game, gathered nine possessions in a rusty display. In horse racing parlance, he'll be better for the run.
THE BIGGEST UPSET
Carlton caused the upset of the round defeating West Coast by seven points at Subiaco Oval on Friday night. The loss was the Eagles third at home this year.
The Blues led all night and, helped along with six goals from regular full back Steve Silvagni and 39 touches from Craig Bradley, withstood a late Eagles' challenge for a gutsy win.
Geelong climbed to second spot on the ladder with a 56-point win over Adelaide at Kardinia Park on Saturday. After a wind assisted six goal to nothing first quarter the Cats were never headed.
With the aid of the breeze in the last term, the Crows were still given a chance to win but were outscored by the Cats and later criticised by coach Malcolm Blight for an "unforgivable" display.
Wayward kicking cost Fremantle any chance of victory over Port Adelaide at Football Park on Saturday night.
The Power consolidated their position in the top three with a 15-point win and look a real chance to make the final eight.
Brisbane had almost twice as many scoring shots as Collingwood but could manage only a 15-point win over the Magpies at the Gabba on Saturday night.

Lions' full forward Jarrod Molloy proved the difference between the two teams with six goals while the Magpies were kept in the game by star midfielders Nathan Buckley and Paul Willams who combined for the goal of the match.
Williams swooped on Buckley's clearance from the full back line and ran through the centre of the ground before kicking the goal from outside 60 metres.
The Magpies have dropped outside the top eight for the first time this season following their fifth straight loss.
*Andrew Bartram is a Melbourne-based journalist.
